## Individual-risk modeling {#sec-pnl-ir}

*This is a recipe for* the **individual risk (IR) model** — a *fixed* block of
policies, each an independent loss — and the lesson it teaches about
*parameterization*. The usual **collective risk** model has a random claim
count; the IR model fixes the count (`dfreq[n]`, `n` policies) and puts a
Bernoulli-style severity on each. Life and other short-duration guarantees are
the canonical case, and they expose a trap: folding the deterministic premium
into a *signed profit severity* reproduces the mean but not the standard
deviation. The `pnl` — premium **less** losses — is the fix, and it is exact.

```{python}
from _setup import *
import numpy as np
```

The whole page reads off one block of parameters — an `n`-life one-year term
book, each life paying face `F` on death (probability `q`) against premium `P`.
Units are reduced by `gcd(P, F)` (true `P=20, F=1000`) so the arithmetic is
tidy:

```{python}
n = 1_000_000     # policies (fixed count -> individual risk model)
q = 0.019         # one-year mortality
P = 1             # premium per life   (gcd-reduced; true 20)
F = 50            # face amount        (gcd-reduced; true 1000)
```

**Beat 1 — the DecL (the tempting, wrong parameterization).** Per-life profit is
`+P` if the life survives and `P − F` if it dies, so the "obvious" model is a
signed severity with atoms `{P−F, P} = {-49, +1}`:

```{python}
naive = f'agg Life dfreq[{n}] dsev[{P-F} {P}] [{q} {1-q}]'
pp(naive)
```

**Beats 2 & 3 — build, validate.** The mean is reproduced exactly; the standard
deviation is not — validation flags `AGG_CV` / `AGG_SKEW` (and the severity
twins):

```{python}
a = build(naive)
print(f'{a.name}: valid = {a.valid}')
qd(a.validation_df)
```

**Why the mean survives but the sd does not — the exact linear fit.** The atoms
`-49` and `+1` are *odd*, so placing them exactly needs `bs = 1`. But (see below)
the aggregate really lives on the spacing-`F = 50` lattice, so the grid sizer
coarsens toward it. On a `bs = 50` grid `{…, -50, 0, 50, …}` neither atom lands,
and mass-preserving (linear) bucketing splits each onto its two neighbors:

```{python}
# atom +1 (prob 1-q) sits 1 above 0, 49 below 50; atom -49 (prob q) sits 1 above
# -50, 49 below 0. Linear split -> mass on {-50, 0, 50}:
xs = np.array([-50, 0, 50])
ps = np.array([q*49/50, (q + (1-q)*49)/50, (1-q)/50])

xt, pt = np.array([P-F, P]), np.array([q, 1-q])        # true atoms

def m12(x, w):
    m1 = (x*w).sum()
    return m1, (x**2*w).sum()

m1_s, m2_s = m12(xs, ps)      # spread severity
m1_t, m2_t = m12(xt, pt)      # true severity
print(f'mean   : spread={m1_s:.4f}  true={m1_t:.4f}   (equal)')
print(f'E[X^2] : spread={m2_s:.4f}  true={m2_t:.4f}   inflated by {m2_s-m2_t:.0f}')
print(f'sd     : spread={np.sqrt(m2_s-m1_s**2):.4f}  true={np.sqrt(m2_t-m1_t**2):.4f}')
```

Linear bucketing is *mean-preserving by construction*, so the first moment is
untouched. But splitting a point mass across a width-`b` bucket at distances
`d₁, d₂` (with `d₁ + d₂ = b`) adds variance exactly `d₁·d₂` — here `1·49 = 49` on
top of `E[X²]`. That single unit of inflation carries all the way through the
`n`-fold convolution, so the aggregate sd is off by the same ratio: the mean
matches to machine precision while the sd is 43% too large.

**The observation: "wasted" space.** The aggregate is
`profit = nP − F·(deaths) = n − 50·(deaths)`, so it is supported *only* on
multiples of 50. At `bs = 1` that means **49 of every 50 buckets are
structurally empty** — a 50× oversampled grid, and exactly where the amplified
round-off "grass" shows up (see `docs/error-analysis.md`). The severity wants a
fine bucket; the aggregate wants a coarse one; and no single grid and origin
serves both, because the deterministic `+P` per life *accumulates* `n` times
under convolution and a one-origin grid cannot carry that shift.

**The fix — reparameterize as a P&L.** Pull the deterministic premium out of the
stochastic severity. Model *losses* with the benefit severity on its natural
`{0, F}` lattice, and let the total premium `nP` enter as an affine shift — which
is precisely what `pnl … premium less agg …` does:

```{python}
loss = f'agg Loss dfreq[{n}] dsev[0 {F}] [{1-q} {q}]'
book = f'pnl Life.PNL {n*P} premium less {loss}'
pp(book)
```

```{python}
b = build(book)
show(b)
```

Now `{0, 50}` is phase-0 and buckets **exactly** at `bs = 50`; the loss
aggregate stays on `50ℤ` (phase-0 is closed under convolution) — no wasted cells,
no grass; and the premium `nP` is an exact affine shift. The margin standard
deviation matches the analytic value to machine precision:

```{python}
analytic_sd = np.sqrt(n * (F**2*q - (F*q)**2))    # Var(profit) = Var(loss)
margin_sd = float(b.summary_df.loc['Margin', 'SD'])
print(f'margin sd: pnl={margin_sd:.6f}  analytic={analytic_sd:.6f}')
```

**Beat 4 — the check.** [Check-Reparameterization]

The lesson generalizes beyond life: an individual-risk book is a *fixed-count*
aggregate of losses, and the numerically clean model keeps the benefit severity
on its own lattice (`{0, F}`) rather than a signed profit severity (`{P−F, P}`).
Deterministic quantities — premium, expenses — belong in the affine `pnl` layer,
not smuggled into the severity. Reproduce the mean **and** the sd; waste no grid.
